To strengthen the IT and Information Management team, we are looking for an Information Security Officer (ISO) in Amersfoort. As ISO, you ensure that our information, systems and processes remain safe and reliable and, together with fellow verifiers, shape the information security policy of Natural Monuments.
Your job as an Information Security Officer
IT and information management are increasingly important for Natural Monuments to achieve its goals. Information security plays a crucial role in this. We work with a lot of information, systems, processes, partners, employees and volunteers. We do it all over the country, spread over 24 management units and a central office. That is why we want to organise our information system secure, reliable and future-proof.
As ISO, you are responsible for the realisation, implementation and monitoring of information security within Natural Monuments. You help the organisation to identify risk derivatives, take management measures and make information security a structural part of policies, projects, suppliers' agreements and daily work processes.
You advise board, management, and fellow officers on information security, IT security and continuity management. You record information security incidents and coordinate their handling. You will also facilitate awareness activities, such as training, campaigns and phishing tests. You work closely with the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Officer.
What are you gonna do?
Information security policy: You will develop information security policies, update them where necessary and help implement them within the organisation.
Advice and implementation: You advise management and colleagues on the translation of information security policy into annual plans, processes, projects and concrete measures.
Risk analysis and follow-up: You investigate incidents and carry out risk analyses in projects and in the standing organisation. You record incidents and threats, advise on measures and monitor the follow-up.
Cooperation with privacy and IT: You work closely with IT and Information Management, the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Officer.
Suppliers and contracts: You assess internal and external parties' reports on relevance to information security and ensure that information security is secured in agreements and contracts with third parties.
Awareness: You facilitate awareness activities, such as phishing tests, trainings and campaigns, so that fellow verifiers handle information safely and carefully.
Incident registration and coordination: You maintain a central record of information security incidents and coordinate their handling.
Continuity management: You help set up and organise business continuity management (including crisis management), including processes, standards and procedures.
Crisis opinion: You advise the crisis team in a hack, cyberattack or other continuity disruption in the service.
The IT and Information Management Department
As an Information Security Officer, you will be transferred to the IT and Information Management department. This department supports the national organisation in the safe, reliable and effective use of information, applications, data and technology.
You work together with colleagues in IT and Information Management, privacy and the various business areas. You also have contact with external suppliers and service providers about security measures, contractual arrangements, processing agreements and their security policy.
The department works flexibly from home and at our headquarters in Amersfoort. You report to the IT and Information Management Manager and have a functional reporting line to the Director of Finance and Business Management. You also answer to the board.
What you're taking
With these qualities you can contribute to a safe, resilient and reliable information provision within Natural Monuments:
Distributed: You have extensive knowledge of information security, IT security and business continuity management. You follow developments in your field and can translate them into policies and practical measures.
Analytical: You can understand risk deficiencies, incidents and vulnerabilities well and come up with clear advice and appropriate improvement measures.
Independent: You are a professional judgment based on facts, risk assessments, policies and laws and regulations. You are clearly dared to advise, even if that is not always the easiest message.
Communication: You can explain complex information security issues clearly and intelligibly to different target groups, from fellow managers to management, management and management.
Connecting: You can easily switch between IT, privacy, management, suppliers and the organization. You create support and help fellow verifiers to make information security practical.
As an association for nature in the Netherlands, we want to represent everyone at Natural Monuments, because we believe that nature is there for us all. A varied function with a lot of impact within the entire organisation. You contribute to a secure, reliable and future-proof information provision and work with relevant fellow verifiers across the country

Hios y Madres del Silencio (Children and Mothers of Silence) is a Chilean non-profit organization that has been working for more than ten years for mothers and families looking for children who were separated from them in the context of forced or irregular adoptions, and for adopted people who are looking for their biological family and identity.
HMS supports search and family reunification, guides stakeholders and works to recognise this issue from a human rights and psychosocial perspective. In addition, the organisation is working on awareness and national and international cooperation.

Ensure that information leads to better decisions and a safer Royal Marechaussee
The Royal Marechaussee is available 24 hours a day for the safety of the Netherlands. To perform this task properly, reliable information is indispensable. Not only to understand what has happened, but precisely to identify risk derivatives in time, to identify developments and to continuously improve the organisation.
Within the Safety, Health and Environment cluster (VGM), we are building the Analysis, Learning & Improve section. As a Strategic Analyst, VGM, you play a key role in that. You will investigate what information the organisation needs, translate complex analyses into strategic insights and ensure that they lead to better decisions and a safer functioning Royal Marechaussee.
Are you analytically strong, curious and are you getting energy from complex issues? Then we'll find you as Strategic Analyst VGM.
What are you gonna do?
As a Strategic Analyst VGM, you are responsible for strategic analyses that contribute to the operational, tactical and strategic decision-making within the Royal Marechaussee. You translate information into insights, advice and concrete improvement measures and thus make an important contribution to the further development of the VGM domain.
You do not start with the information that happens to be available, but with the question of what information is needed to reach a good decision. Together with clients, you will identify the information needs, plan and determine which analytical methods and sources of information are needed. In addition to what is happening now, you also look at what developments and potential risk derivatives can occur.
Then you bring together information from different sources, create links and translate your analyses into clear advice, concrete improvement measures or lessons identified. You will also investigate whether measures taken actually have the desired effect. For example, analyzing trends in safety notifications, audit findings, risk inventories and evaluations and other relevant sources of information. By combining these insights you can make visible where risk derivatives arise, what measures work and where additional actions are needed.
In complex investigations, you do not act as research leader. You will be able to join the coordinator of the Research Committees on the plan, quality and results of the research. From your analytical role, you help to put research findings in the right context and translate them into relevant insights for the organisation.
You also contribute to the development of analytical methods, information products and the Lessons Learned process, so that insights are not kept on their own but are secured sustainably within the organisation. You will work closely with fellow RFs within VGM, the Intelligence Organisation, other defence components and external chain partners.

What are you gonna do?
The PhD research focuses on the relationship between body composition, treatment response and survival in patients with pancreatic cancer(PDAC). In doing so, you will investigate which tumour characteristics are associated with changes in body composition and clinical outcomes. For this, you combine clinical data and patient material with transcriptomics, imaging mass cytometry and CT-based analyses. The aim is to identify tumour-related factors that may provide new targets for future treatments.
Your main tasks are:
Collection and processing of clinical data, imaging data and patient material from various Dutch medical centers.
Performing omics analyses, spatial imaging and statistical and bioinformatical analyses.
Establishment and coordination of a translational research infrastructure
Developing new prognostic models.
Writing scientific publications and presenting research results at national and international conferences.
The findings can be validated with prospectively collected biomaterials and extensively characterized patient cohorts within the international ONCOVERS consortium.
Where are you going to work?
The Research Laboratory of the department of Stomach, Darm and Liver Diseases is the home of this PhD research. From the LUMC you work intensively with researchers from Amsterdam UMC and Maastricht UMC+. The research is embedded in ONCoverse, a large international research consortium that wants to better understand the biological complexity of pancreatic cancer and improve patient treatment.
An important basis for the research is the national biobank infrastructure for pancreatic cancer. This contains material from over 3,000 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), collected within the Pearl SNOER initiative. The combination of these patient cohorts, prospectively collected biomaterials and collaboration between different research centres offers a strong translational research environment.
Cooperation is central to the project. Researchers, analysts and surgeons from different centres bring together their expertise and there are contacts with researchers at home and abroad. How do you organise and finance cooperation between care and social domain so that it works sustainably? As a researcher funding domain-wide collaboration (MOVE) at the research group BUNDLE of the Health Campus The Hague, LUMC you will explore this current issue in first-line care. You connect scientific research with experiences of professionals, policy makers and other stakeholders in practice. This way you develop as a researcher, build a broad network and contribute to knowledge that is directly applicable in policy and practice.
What are you gonna do?
Research into the appropriate funding of cross-border cooperation in primary care is central. You will work on how to organise and finance cooperation between general practitioners, community care, social domain, long-term care and regional partners on a sustainable basis. You are part of the national MOVE consortium, which investigates how close neighbourhood associations and regional first-line partnerships can be strengthened. Together with the MOVE research team you will investigate what works for whom, under what circumstances and how this knowledge can be translated into concrete tools for policy and practice.
Specifically, you focus on the role of funding in cross-border cooperation. Current funding is divided into different laws, domains and accountability systems, while in practice cooperation requires joint commitment and shared responsibility. This can create bottlenecks, such as the wrong-pocket problem: Investment and revenue are not always shared by the same party. You will investigate which funding mechanisms support or hinder cooperation and how appropriate funding can contribute to sustainable cooperation in the first line.
Your time is roughly equal between these two parts: Half of you spend on the MOVE investigation, the other half on other tasks within BUNDLE. There is also room to spend some of your time on research, personal development or projects you choose.
Your main tasks are:
Perform literature research and qualitative case studies in regions where the co-operation develops in practice.
Interviews by professionals, policy makers and other stakeholders on what they need and on what funding incentives help or hinder cooperation.
Analyse research data and translate insights into useful recommendations, reports, practical products and scientific publications.
Contribute to various work for BUNDLE, including helping to design research into alternative funding, education for the master's Population Health Management (to a limited extent), preparing and notifying consultation, co-thinking and writing about grant and project proposals, guiding the onboarding of new colleagues, maintaining contact with external cooperation partners, and (co-) assisting students or trainees.
Where are you going to work?
The research group BUNDLE, the Academic Expertise Centre for Alternative Cost Management in the Netherlands, is part of Health Campus The Hague. BUNDLE develops, collects and shares scientific knowledge about alternative forms of funding in healthcare, with attention to development, implementation and evaluation. The focus is on funding that contributes to accessible, affordable and good care. BUNDLE consists of a group of enthusiastic researchers and values an open and informal atmosphere.
Health Campus The Hague of the LUMC works from a broad health perspective on research, education and practical solutions for better health and care. Within this environment you work at the intersection of science, policy and practice, with short lines to healthcare organisations, financiers, knowledge institutes and regional cooperation partners.
You work closely with the MOVE core team and partners within the national consortium. This consortium consists of academic workshops, knowledge institutes, colleges, universities and practical partners in the field of general care, community care, social domain, long-term care and regional support. This gives you the opportunity to develop, learn, build a broad network and contribute to research with direct societal relevance.
What are you taking?
Curiosity about complex issues combine with pleasure in contact with practice. In conversations with different stakeholders you listen carefully and you can translate practical experiences into sharp research insights. You analyse issues carefully, work structured and take initiative. There is no need to be an expert in funding: It is important that you look into this and understand why cooperation in healthcare is sometimes difficult and how funding can make this cooperation more possible. Some years of research experience, for example as a junior researcher or at the end of a PhD course, is a pre.
In addition, you have:
A MSc degree in health economics, Population Health Management, health sciences, public administration, policy and management in healthcare or a similar field of expertise.
Interested in funding, contracting, primary care and domain-wide cooperation.
Experience with qualitative research methods, such as interviews and thematic analysis; experience with Atlas.ti or NVivo is a pre.
Affinity with organisational and coordinating tasks.
Good control of the Dutch and English language, both written and oral. Two or more years of relevant work experience in research, policy or practice on funding is a pre, but not a requirement.

About the Louis Bolk Institute
The Louis Bolk Institute has been an independent knowledge institute for 50 years and we are now with about 85 colleagues. The Louis Bolk Institute is committed to a resilient, healthy and fair agricultural, food and health system. Our unique research approach of looking differently and seeing sharper, ensures that we work on solutions that bring about changes at system level. Researchers are working to strengthen natural systems and processes, whether they are agricultural areas, a company, a patient or a city district. By developing knowledge and seeing it in connection with the dynamic coherence of practice, we make impact. The scientific knowledge we develop is applicable in policy and practice, both for the conventional side of the spectrum and also for the frontrunners. Important clients include ministries, provinces, municipalities, water boards, European Commission, health and welfare organisations and nature organisations. The Louis Bolk Institute is an ANBI foundation based in Bunnik.
What are you going to do as researcher Sustainable Soil Management?
As a researcher Sustainable Soil Management, you work on sustainable soil management issues in the arable and vegetable farming sector. In a team of 18 soil researchers, you will jointly conduct research projects for the national and provincial authorities, farmers, the EU, companies and other organisations. You will investigate how sustainable soil management and soil health can contribute to the practice of agriculture and in relation to societal challenges related to resilient crops, climate adaptation and mitigation and water assessments. Within various projects, you work together with both common, biological and regenerative farmers. Examples of research questions you can think of are:
• How can practical measures applied by the farmer on his/her holding contribute to a resilient soil?
• What is the role of soil life in mineralisation and buffering of soil nitrogen, and can the farmer respond to this in order to reduce nitrogen emissions?
• What monitoring is needed to monitor changes in soil and water quality successfully?
• How can we reduce risk derivatives of soil compaction?
• What opportunities does organic or regenerative agriculture offer to offer new prospects for agriculture?
What do we ask of you as researcher Sustainable Soil Management?
You are an expert and passionate practice-oriented soil researcher, with a heart for both science and agricultural practice. You will carry out research and demonstration projects (possibly as project leader). You organise meetings and share knowledge with farmers, but also with other stakeholders such as (local) governments or interest groups. You collect research data (e.g. through fieldwork), analyse and interpret them and process them in reports and both practical and scientific publications. In addition, you are also jointly responsible for acquiring new research projects, developing substantive (part) theme performances and research lines. Affinity and knowledge about nitrogen processes in soil, experience and affinity with (soil) models (see e.g. www.NDICEA.eu) and/or experience with the analysis of larger (multi-year) datasets are a preview.

The Cognitive Science & Artificial Intelligence Research Center of Tilburg University is carrying out the Secure Hardware Intelligence Extraction and Logic Destruction (SHIELD) research project. This scientific project focuses on AI-supported reverse engineering of integrated circuits, with hardware assurance, threat analysis and intelligence analysis applications.
The project is being carried out within the research lines in the field of Deep Learning for Perception and Data Science and Safety and Security, in collaboration with the Data Science Centre of Excellence of the Dutch Defence Academy and the Netherlands Forensic Institute (NFI). In this function you work on the interface of computer vision, micro-electronic analysis and hardware security. You work under the guidance of researchers within the Department of Intelligent Systems.
You are formally appointed to the Department of Intelligent Systems (DIS) and work closely with the Department of Computational Cognitive Science (DCS).
The project
The SHIELD project is a collaboration between Tilburg University, the Data Science Centre of Excellence of the Dutch Defence Academy and the Netherlands Forensic Institute. The project brings together expertise in the fields of artificial intelligence, micro-electronic analysis and hardware security. The aim is to develop AI-supported methods for reverse engineering of integrated circuits, supporting hardware assurance, threat analysis and intelligence analysis processes.
Within the project you will develop a methodology for analysing microscopic images with a high resolution of integrated circuits. In addition, you combine computer vision, deep learning and techniques for logical reconstruction. You will investigate how different imaging techniques including scanning electron microscope (SEM), photon emission microscope (PEM) and focused ion beam (FIB) imaging - can be combined with AI to reconstruct chip structures on a nanoscale and derive the effect of a chip from the physical layout.
A key challenge is to obtain reliable structural and logical information from complex semiconductor architectures, while available image data may be related to noise, limited image quality and other practical limitations.
You focus in particular on the following three main tasks:
(a) developing deep-learning pipelines for multi-chip segmenting and nanoscale classification of transistors based on microscopic images;
(b) developing graph-based inference models that allow higher-level logical blocks to be reconstructed and identified deviant structures that may indicate Hardware Trojans;
(c) evaluating methods for reading and reconstructing memory content, analysing vulnerabilities and reconstructing logical structures based on image data directly linked to the physical chip structure.
You will investigate how AI-controlled analysis can automate the current, largely manual reverse engineering process. In doing so, you develop methods to extract relevant features from microscopic images and to interpret the underlying structure of a chip. The developed methods must also be robust against noise, obfuscation and differences between chip architectures. Because research is at the intersection of scientific innovation and hardware security, there is a lot of attention to responsible handling of sensitive datasets and forensic framework conditions. You are working on methodological renewal and taking into account the requirements for research into sensitive hardware and data. The ultimate objective of the project is to develop a reproducible proof-of-concept methodology for larger-scale analysis of integrated circuits. The methodology shall be applicable for both defensive hardware verification and information analysis of seized electronic equipment. You will investigate the scientific validity and limitations of the developed methods and contribute to open-access publications and technical documentation. The SHIELD project has a forward-looking research vision and aims to contribute to the strengthening of long-term capabilities in the areas of reliable hardware, semiconductor sovereignty and cyber-electromagnetic resilience.
You mainly work within the AI research infrastructure of Tilburg University. You will be involved in algorithm development, model training and validation of the developed methods. The experimental validation and image data are based on collaborations with specialised forensic and defence partners. Dutch Forensic

The understandable and appropriate communication of risks to the target group is an important condition for effective disease control. Do you want to understand how risk communication can better match the needs of different groups of citizens and how best to communicate about different types of risk derivatives? Research on risk communication on infectious diseases
Understandable and transparent communication that matches the target group is indispensable for effective disease control. In this promotional process you will investigate how risk communication can better match the needs of different groups of citizens, and how you can communicate optimally about various types of risk derivatives. You will investigate a conceptual framework through a mixed-methods approach and apply it to concrete practical examples such as tick bites, vaccination or population surveys. You can translate the findings into a convenient decision model for healthcare, policy and communication professionals, which directly contributes to the daily practice of public health.
The research project consists of four subprojects:
Performing a systematic literature research and developing a theoretical framework.
Doing in-depth qualitative research among experts and citizens to explore information needs, knowledge and attitudes.
The development of experimental research into the effects of different forms of communication on, among other things, risk perception, trust and compliance.
Translating the results into a workable system for practice, that you then test with professionals.
As a PhD candidate, you are responsible for the conduct of this research and the analysis of the data. The PhD research covers various socio-scientific methodological approaches. This way you will set up and conduct literature research, focus groups, and experimental research. You have a key role in each of the sub-projects and develop as an expert in risk communication on infectious diseases.
You write at least five scientific articles for international peer reviewed journals and present your results at national and international conferences, resulting in a dissertation. In addition, you translate your findings into concrete policy advice. You will become an expert in risk communication and will be given the space to take courses to further strengthen your research skills. You will work with an interdisciplinary guidance team with expertise in infectious disease control, risk perception and behavioural change. Open Science is the movement that stands for a more open research practice. It is assumed that open science improves the reproducibility, honesty and reliability of scientific results. The Netherlands Forensic Institute (NFI) provides high-quality forensic services using state-of-the-art technology and science. Team Microtracks & Materials (M&M) plays a leading role in forensic investigations of various types of crime.
Team M&M conducts forensic research into various materials such as shot residue, glass, paint, fibres and unknown materials. We are constantly working to align our processes with the wishes of the Dutch criminal justice chain. We want to support the police with information during the search and the identification of traces during the phase of the evidence so that the judge can make a proper ruling in a court of law. For an initial picture of the research, you could read this article:
What can gunshot residue tell us about a shooting? . . NFI - Dutch Forensic Institute
In addition to criminal investigations, the NFI is also a state knowledge institution. In this role we are also working on the development of the future of forensic research. For one of our R&D projects we are looking for an enthusiastic and skilled project worker for one year, with successful results this can be extended by one year.
New Light for Scotchesten Research
Shot crime investigation is an important part of the investigation in shooting incidents. A new reagent quickly makes lead-containing shot residue visible at the scene, giving new possibilities for testing shot residue. Team M&M is about to start preparing this reagent for structural deployment at the scene by the Forensic Investigation. This research is financed from strategic funds from the Dutch Police and the Public Prosecutor's Office. We will test the method extensively for various purposes, including the operation on different substrates and under conditions. The operation will then be validated, after which the application of a test kit together with the Forensic Investigation will be arrested.
In addition to this research aimed at carrying out tests at the crime scene quickly, we also enter the (forensic) depth in this project, in case of successful validation. We will investigate how visualizations can contribute to our understanding of where shot residue ends up and how they move in time and space. Both during and immediately after shootings, but also over longer periods of time or when indirectly contacting a shooter. This will help to improve the quality of the reconstruction of shooting incidents and research at activity level in the future

As a PhD student, you will investigate how we can better predict, diagnose and treat heart failure in children with hereditary heart muscle diseases. You focus on dilatating cardiomyopathy (DCM), a rare but severe cardiac muscle disease that can lead to heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias and premature death. Although treatment is currently largely symptomatic, new, more targeted therapies are being developed internationally. To enable these developments, a thorough understanding of the disease, genetic causes and factors affecting the quality of life is needed.
The research is part of the national PRECISE consortium and is carried out in close collaboration with patient organisations and a wide network of doctors and researchers from other UMCs in the Netherlands.
Within this promotional process you will focus on different research lines:
You will contribute to a rural infrastructure for research into DCM at child age by integrating clinical, genetic and imaging data into a national database.
You will investigate which early characteristics predict which children develop a more serious course, with special attention to genetic factors, echocardiographic and other imaging parameters, and additional disorders.
You study the yield and clinical impact of modern genetic diagnostics, including short-read and long-read whole genome sequencing, in patients where no genetic cause could be identified until now.
You evaluate the diagnosis and treatment of children with a suspicion of myocardiitis, with the aim of developing nationwide diagnostic and treatment protocols.
You will explore with patients and parents which factors affect the quality of life of children and young adults with DCM, so that we can improve patient guidance focused in the coming years.
You will also translate research results into scientific publications and present them at national and international conferences. This not only builds new knowledge, but also a valuable scientific network.

Excellent mastery of the Dutch and English language, both orally and in writing.

As a data scientist you build and modernise the data pipelines that map antibiotic resistance in the Netherlands. In this role you combine the deepening of complex data puzzles in R with the dynamics of close collaboration with epidemiologists and medical specialists. You will be given the freedom to smartly restructure existing SAS processes to scalable code. Within a socially driven environment, you develop yourself at the intersection of data science and epidemiology, while your work contributes to decisions on national public health. What are you gonna do?
As a data scientist, you work on mapping antibiotic resistance in the Netherlands. RIVM collects data through the Infectious Disease Surveillance Information System . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . In this system data from the daily diagnostics of Dutch medical and microbiological laboratories come together. You build, modernise and automate the data streams and pipelines that make these raw laboratory data clear.
Most of the week you work within the department of Healthcare-related Infections and Anti-bacterial Resistance (ZIA). Together with epidemiologists, you convert existing data pipelines that are still running in SAS to the programming language R. You write scripts for data transformation and translate data into clear tables, graphs, maps and reports. A concrete result of this work can be seen in the annual overviews of the NethMap One Health 2025 report.
About one day a week you join your immediate fellow data scientists in the Data, Innovation and Surveillance (DIS) department. Within DIS you will work on technically strengthening the packages and standards that the entire center of Epidemiology and Surveillance of Infectious Diseases (EPI) uses. You can use tools such as Tidyverse for data pipelines, GitLab for version management, R Markdown for automatic reporting and R Shiny for dashboards.
What your work looks like in practice: You will explore a series of complex SAS scripts used to interpret laboratory results. With your experience in R you can see how this process can be faster and where duplicate work is done. You design generic functions to combine these processes and align this approach with the epidemiologists involved. When it turns out that different laboratories deliver their data just differently, you adjust the code. You recognize the patterns in the different data and build up the R functions so that they can handle these differences flexibly. This way you can ensure reliable and reusable code that meets our internal quality standards.
In this work you will be given the space to renew, which gives you plenty of opportunity to build up knowledge and expertise at the intersection of epidemiology and data science. Your work is directly about monitoring antibiotic resistance in the Netherlands. At RIVM, almost 3,000 fellow officers work together every day to take care of tomorrow. This vacuum has been recommended by the section Epidemiology, Faculty of Health, Medicine and Life Sciences.
The department of Epidemiology at Maastricht University is looking for a PhD student for the scientific research into 'The clock is ticking: The role of disturbances in circadian rhythms in the onset of long-term fatigue in people treated for colon cancer'.
FUNCTIONAL DEVICE
Long-term fatigue is one of the most commonly reported symptoms in people treated for colorectal cancer (thickness cancer) and these symptoms have a major impact on their quality of life. To develop effective interventions to reduce fatigue symptoms, a better understanding of the underlying biological processes leading to long-term fatigue after cancer is needed. Recent research shows that disturbances of circadian rhythms (day-night rhythms) may play an important role in the development of cancer-related fatigue. However, little research has been done on people treated for colorectal cancer.
The first objective of this project is to investigate the role of disturbances in circadian rhythms in the development of long-term fatigue in people treated for colorectal cancer. For this purpose, data will be collected within an ongoing prospective cohort study: EnCoRe study (www.encorestudie.nl). For this study, patients with colorectal cancer are recruited on diagnosis and monitored with repeated measurements up to 5 years after cancer treatment. Disturbances in circadian rhythms will be extensively mapped by measuring day-night rhythms of activity and rest (accelerometer data), sleep duration and sleep quality (self-reported), and by measuring cortisol levels throughout the day (in saliva). Do you want to understand why therapy works, apart from the specific technique used? Do you have an interest in the psychological processes that determine how people react to treatment, such as expectations of treatment, environment, motivation and treatment relationship? Do you want to contribute to both fundamental scientific insights and the development of clinical applications? Then we invite you to apply for this four-year PhD program.
In this project you combine experimental research into psychological and neurobiological mechanisms with practical research within military mental health care. You work on insights that are both scientifically innovative and have clinical impact.
We are looking for a PhD student who is not only curious about existing knowledge, but also actively dares to ask new questions. In this project you will have the space to develop your own scientific hypotheses and shape the research.
The project consists of two complementary pillars:
Application-oriented research:
How can we make treatments more effective without changing the treatment itself? In this project you will investigate how psychological and contextual factors around a treatment can be consciously used to increase the effectiveness of psychotherapy. What factors can we influence and to what extent do they contribute to recovery? You develop an applicable intervention for the treatment practice and test how much this treatment outcomes can change.
Experimental study:
In this line of research, the main focus is on unravelling underlying mechanisms. How, for example, do expectations influence what people think and experience? In this project you will conduct experimental studies combining psychological theories with behavioural research and neurobiological measurements to understand how people react to and give meaning to their environment. For example, you will investigate how expectations, motivation and previous experiences affect emotions, cognitive performance and brain reactions. You also look at individual differences: Why does something work better on one than on the other? The aim is not to improve treatment directly, but to better understand how these fundamental mechanisms work.

As ISO, you ensure that our information, systems and processes remain safe and reliable and, together with fellow verifiers, shape the information security policy of Natural Monuments.
Your job as an Information Security Officer
IT and information management are increasingly important for Natural Monuments to achieve its goals. Information security plays a crucial role in this. We work with a lot of information, systems, processes, partners, employees and volunteers. We do it all over the country, spread over 24 management units and a central office. That is why we want to organise our information system secure, reliable and future-proof.
As ISO, you are responsible for the realisation, implementation and monitoring of information security within Natural Monuments. You help the organisation to identify risk derivatives, take management measures and make information security a structural part of policies, projects, suppliers' agreements and daily work processes.
You advise board, management, and fellow officers on information security, IT security and continuity management. You record information security incidents and coordinate their handling. You will also facilitate awareness activities, such as training, campaigns and phishing tests. You work closely with the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Officer.
What are you gonna do?
Information security policy: You will develop information security policies, update them where necessary and help implement them within the organisation.
Advice and implementation: You advise management and colleagues on the translation of information security policy into annual plans, processes, projects and concrete measures.
Risk analysis and follow-up: You investigate incidents and carry out risk analyses in projects and in the standing organisation. You record incidents and threats, advise on measures and monitor the follow-up.
Cooperation with privacy and IT: You work closely with IT and Information Management, the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Officer.
Suppliers and contracts: You assess internal and external parties' reports on relevance to information security and ensure that information security is secured in agreements and contracts with third parties.
Awareness: You facilitate awareness activities, such as phishing tests, trainings and campaigns, so that fellow verifiers handle information safely and carefully.
Incident registration and coordination: You maintain a central record of information security incidents and coordinate their handling.
Continuity management: You help set up and organise business continuity management (including crisis management), including processes, standards and procedures.
Crisis opinion: You advise the crisis team in a hack, cyberattack or other continuity disruption in the service.

Tuberculosis has a mysterious protein secretion system, ESX-4, which can be lethal to the bacteria itself in activation. We're going to unravel how ESX-4 is regulated, with the aim of discovering a way to let the bacteria shut itself down. Mycobacterium tuberculosis has an impenetrable cell wall. To functionalize this cell wall, the bacteria has five different protein secretion systems, also called ESX systems. Some of these systems are essential for the growth or virulence of the bacteria. However, we know little about ESX-4. Recently, we have discovered that the production of this system is precisely regulated by the peptide WerA and the regulator WerB. Disabling these proteins leads to strong activation of ESX-4 and the production of various possible toxins. This activation is harmful to the bacteria itself. In this project you will investigate the function of these possible toxins. In addition, you unravel which signal and which mechanism are responsible for the induction of ESX-4. Eventually, we want to disrupt this system, which may cause tuberculosis to poison itself. We conduct this research in collaboration with Radboud University, where a PhD candidate for this project is also appointed. The project is funded by NWO. You will conduct laboratory research into the functioning and regulation of the ESX-4 system in pathogenic mycobacteria. Your work will include: Experimenting with bacterial cultures. Performing genetic and molecular analyses. Working with microscopy. Analyzing data, including proteomics and transcriptomics data. Studying proteins, including possible toxins. Many experiments are carried out with the model organism Mycobacterium marinum. You also investigate the tuberculosis bacteria itself, a BSL-3 organism. Here's what you're gonna do.
Which curious and multidisciplinary researcher wants to discover how humans, groundwater and landscapes have influenced each other in the past? Develop and use innovative digital research methods and develop your research into a dissertation over the past four years.
What are you gonna do?
How did changing groundwater levels in the past affect people's living and how they used the landscape? And how did people adapt when their environment became wetter or drier? We still know surprisingly little about this interaction between groundwater, landscape and human activity in the past. In the project Living with Groundwater you will change this.
As a researcher, you will spend four years in the relationship between groundwater, habitation and land use in the Netherlands in the period from 1000 before to 1000 after the beginning of our year. Archaeology is your starting point. You combine large amounts of data from various archaeological, historical and earth science sources and explore groundwater trends and patterns in habitation and land use. This way you can reconstruct changes in groundwater over time and investigate how these are related to changes in habitation and land use.
An important part of your research is the development and application of innovative digital research methods. This unlocks, combines, integrates and analyzes large amounts of structured and unstructured data. For example, techniques for text and image analysis, spatial analysis and modelling. You will work in a multidisciplinary team with researchers from the Landscape and Archaeology departments.
During the project you will be accompanied by content and scientific guidance and will be given plenty of space to develop as a researcher, publish research results and present your work to a scientific and wider audience. The four-year research is the basis for a dissertation, for which you are associated as an outside doctoral candidate at a Dutch university.

Policy colleagues, the official summit and directors: They can all count on your clear administrative-legal advice. As a senior lawyer, you are at the table with the people who decide about the future of the Netherlands. Think of important themes such as PFAS, Tata Steel, fireworks, air quality or sustainable transport. You also advise on how to take the healthy environment and the protection of the environment into account when looking for solutions to major issues such as housing or the deployment of the armed forces. You want to know how you can make an impact? Then read on quickly.
How you contribute
Your work is very diverse. You are working on a compensation scheme for fireworks dealers who experience adverse effects from the new fireworks ban or you are ensuring that European rules on emissions (emissions) from large factories are properly incorporated into the Dutch legal system. In addition, you will receive many legal questions from policy makers, directors, citizens and executives throughout the week, and it is up to you to answer them. Often that answer will be based on the Environmental Management Act or the Environmental Act, but you also have to regularly dig into other laws to find answers.
As a lawyer in a ministry, you work in a political environment. That means your agenda is often determined by what's going on in society. Is there any new information available on the emissions of very worrying substances from the Tata Steel steelworks? Then you can count on questions coming from the media or the House of Representatives and you must help to answer them urgently. Do municipalities indicate to the executive that they are concerned about the transport of dangerous substances by trains passing through their cities? Then there's a good chance you'll have to clear your agenda to prepare a meeting and outline the legal frameworks.
Your work
You advise on the legal possibilities in developing policies and drafting new legislation.
You proactively think along with policy makers and steer from a legal perspective.
You will be interviewing stakeholders inside and outside the department to provide your advice or to obtain information needed when drafting regulations. Together with your policy colleague, you represent the position of the Ministry.
You draw up (legal) opinions and notes for directors and write laws and regulations.

More at National Water and Soil Traineeship
Are you a newly graduated Hbo or wo-worf with passion for the rural area? Are you ready to make a meaningful contribution to the great transition challenges of this time? Then the National Traineeship Rural Area (NTLG) is exactly what you're looking for!
About the traineeship
With the NTLG we offer you a flying start in the field of rural areas: the place where large transitions around nitrogen, biodiversity, nature and climate come together. An effective approach to these transitions requires a new generation of professionals with a fresh and broad look . You can be this! Essentially, you learn to look beyond the boundaries of your own organization and assignment. That is why our two-year trainee program offers space for both substantive and personal development, which benefits both you and the trainee and the organisation you work on.
You will get started with various themes such as the transition of agriculture, broad prosperity and spatial planning, and will have the opportunity to visit various organisations together with your fellow trainees and build a valuable network. In addition, you will participate with your trainee group in a reality game that you will play for two years and in which you will work on challenging issues in an interactive and effective way.
This is what you're going to do as a trainee area development . .
If you walk, cycle, sail or drive in the rural area of Drenthe and Groningen, you will soon find Prolander. Prolander's main task is to realize the Netherlands Nature Network. This network strengthens and connects important nature reserves. Together with regional partners, Prolander is looking for solutions that contribute to strong nature and perspective for agriculture. There is also attention to water storage and recreation. Prolander is working on a major social issue: How do we ensure a sustainable future for the rural area?
To make that future possible, much must be done behind the scenes. Think of acquiring land, advising on subsidies, creating spatial designs, jointly drawing up layout plans and the actual layout of an area. At Prolander you work with more than 150 colleagues on the whole process: from design to realization.
One of these challenges is the programme Growing Coast . Within this programme, Prolander is responsible for the elaboration and implementation of Pillar 1: raising agricultural land with sludge from the Ems-Dollard. The project has a long run, but is still at the beginning of its implementation. There is therefore plenty of room to think with and shape the approach. For this project we are looking for a trainee who likes to pioneer, take initiative and like to switch between different interests and organisations.
Project objective
Within the programme Me Growing Coast sludge is extracted from the Eems-Dollard and used to raise agricultural land in the area. This will raise the ground level. This improves the conditions for agriculture and offers opportunities to increase water levels, protect peat and counter-pressure salt torment.
